Adult Fusca drum (Umbrina ronchus) attain a considerable size, with the ultimate total length recorded at 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], placing this species among the larger members of the Sciaenidae. This maximum body length was derived from field surveys of the oldest individuals encountered in coastal waters. A length-weight regression applied to these data yields an asymptotic wet weight of 13,182 grams [Wwi = 13,182 grams], reflecting the robust, deep-bodied morphology typical of the genus. Comparative data from related Umbrina species suggest that this size range is consistent with a relatively slow growth trajectory and a prolonged reproductive lifespan. The species is characterized by a laterally compressed body, a subterminal mouth equipped with barbels, and a silvery-grey coloration with oblique dark stripes running along the flanks. Size at first maturity, however, is substantially smaller, as evidenced by the total length at puberty reaching only 28.7 centimeters [Lp = 28.7 centimeters], which marks the point at which gonadal recrudescence commences in maturing individuals.

Early life history in Fusca drum begins with a notably small propagule. The wet weight at birth is estimated from the typical egg diameter of approximately 0.8 millimeters for this species, yielding a value of approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams]. Such a minute initial mass is characteristic of sciaenids that produce pelagic, yolk-sac larvae dependent on endogenous reserves prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. Following eclosion from the fertilised ovum, the yolk-sac larva undergoes a brief endotrophic phase during which it absorbs its yolk supply before the trophic switch to active planktonic foraging. The transition to the free-swimming, exogenously feeding larva marks the commencement of rapid somatic growth. The body mass at puberty, by contrast, is substantially greater, with wet weight at puberty estimated at 282 grams [Wwp = 282 grams], a threshold that aligns with the attainment of sufficient energy stores to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C], reproductive output in this species was assessed. At this thermal regime, females produce an average of approximately 5,000 to 10,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5,000 to 10,000 eggs per spawning event] and undergo multiple spawning episodes per year [F_R_i = multiple spawning episodes per year]. The high daily fecundity, when integrated over a spawning season, underscores the species' capacity for substantial reproductive effort. The daily reproductive rate is influenced by a combination of factors including female body size, nutritional condition, and water temperature, with cooler conditions generally prolonging the vitellogenic cycle. The spawning period in the wild typically coincides with the warmer months, though captive populations maintained at 17.3 °C exhibit year-round reproductive activity. The fecundity estimates were derived from counts of hydrated oocytes in gravid females and corroborated by egg trap collections in mesocosm experiments.

Longevity data for Fusca drum indicate a maximum lifespan of 7,300 days [am = 7,300 days] under natural environmental conditions, based on tag-recapture studies and otolith annulus readings from the oldest documented individuals at a temperature of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C]. This duration is typical for a sciaenid of this body size, with larger species in the family often living for several decades. The age-related mortality pattern appears to follow a gradual increase in senescence rather than a sharp post-reproductive decline, as iteroparous adults continue spawning across multiple seasons. The temperature regime experienced throughout life, averaging around 17.3 °C in the study region, is thought to influence metabolic rate and thereby the pace of ageing. Individuals inhabiting warmer peripheral waters may exhibit slightly reduced longevity compared to those in the cooler core of the species' distribution, though the observed differences fall within the range of natural variation.

The ecological role of Fusca drum within its coastal habitat is that of a benthic predator, foraging primarily on crustaceans, polychaete worms, and small molluscs. This feeding ecology is reflected in its body plan, with the relatively large ultimate wet weight of 13,182 grams [Wwi = 13,182 grams] conferring a competitive advantage when exploiting dense prey patches. Juveniles, by contrast, rely on smaller zooplankton and are therefore restricted to shallow nursery grounds such as seagrass beds and estuarine margins, where they grow rapidly toward the total length at puberty of 28.7 centimeters [Lp = 28.7 centimeters]. The species exhibits a degree of sexual dimorphism in size, with females typically attaining larger asymptotic lengths than males, a pattern consistent with the greater energetic investment required for egg production. Population structure is influenced by fishing pressure, which selectively removes larger individuals and thereby truncates the size distribution, potentially affecting the reproductive potential of the stock.
